:::{#thm-normal-equations}
#### Least squares solutions solve the normal equations

Let $\matr{A}$ be $m \times n$ and $\vecf{b} \in \reals^m$.

1. $\hat{\vecf{x}}$ is a least squares solution (@def-least-squares)
   exactly when it solves the normal equations
   $\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \tp{\matr{A}} \vecf{b}$.
2. The normal equations are consistent (@def-consistent-system).
3. Every least squares solution gives the same fitted vector $\matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}}$:
   the orthogonal projection of $\vecf{b}$ onto $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ (@def-orthogonal-projection).
4. The least squares solution is unique exactly when $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = n$,
   and then $\hat{\vecf{x}} = (\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A})^{-1} \tp{\matr{A}} \vecf{b}$.

:::

::: proof

Let $\vecf{u}$ be the orthogonal projection of $\vecf{b}$ onto $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.
The vectors $\matr{A} \vecf{x}$, as $\vecf{x}$ ranges over $\reals^n$,
are exactly the points of $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ (@def-column-space).
By @thm-closest-point, $\vecf{u}$ is the one point of $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$
closest to $\vecf{b}$, so:

$$
\hat{\vecf{x}} \text{ is a least squares solution}
\iff \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \vecf{u}.
$$

**Parts 1 and 3.**
$\matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \vecf{u}$ holds exactly when
$\vecf{b} - \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} \in \mathcal{C}(\matr{A})^\perp$:
if $\matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \vecf{u}$, then $\vecf{b} - \vecf{u} \in \mathcal{C}(\matr{A})^\perp$
(@def-orthogonal-projection);
conversely, if $\vecf{b} - \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} \in \mathcal{C}(\matr{A})^\perp$,
then $\vecf{b} = \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} + (\vecf{b} - \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}})$
is a split into $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ and $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})^\perp$,
so $\matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \vecf{u}$ by the uniqueness in @thm-orthogonal-direct-sum.
And $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})^\perp = \mathcal{N}(\tp{\matr{A}})$ (@thm-complement-null-space), where

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{A}}\,(\vecf{b} - \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}})
&= \tp{\matr{A}} \vecf{b} - \tp{\matr{A}}\,(\matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}})
&& \text{(@thm-scalar-matmul)}
\\
&= \tp{\matr{A}} \vecf{b} - \tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}},
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\ea
$$

which is $\vzero_n$ exactly when the normal equations hold.

**Part 2.**
$\vecf{u} \in \mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$, so $\vecf{u} = \matr{A} \vecf{x}_0$ for some $\vecf{x}_0$
(@def-column-space), and $\vecf{x}_0$ is a least squares solution,
so it solves the normal equations by part 1.

**Part 4.**
The least squares solutions are exactly the solutions of $\matr{A} \vecf{x} = \vecf{u}$,
a consistent system,
so there is exactly one when $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = n$
and more than one otherwise (@cor-solution-unique).
When $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = n$, $\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}$ is invertible (@thm-gram-invertible),
and multiplying the normal equations on the left by its inverse gives the formula
(@def-matrix-inverse, @thm-identity).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-normal-equations}
#### A least squares line

Fit $y = x_1 + x_2\,t$ to the points $(t, y) = (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2)$:
$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ (the $\mX$ of @exm-gram-invertible)
and $\vecf{b} = (1, 2, 2)$.
$\matr{A}$ has rank $2$, so the solution is unique.
$\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}$ has inverse
$\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ (@exm-gram-invertible),
and $\tp{\matr{A}} \vecf{b} = (1 + 2 + 2,\; 1 + 4 + 6) = (5, 11)$, so

$$
\hat{\vecf{x}}
= \frac{1}{6} \paren{14 \cd 5 - 6 \cd 11,\; -6 \cd 5 + 3 \cd 11}
= \frac{1}{6}\,(4, 3)
= \paren{\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{1}{2}}.
$$

The fitted values are $\matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \paren{\tfrac{7}{6}, \tfrac{5}{3}, \tfrac{13}{6}}$,
and the residuals $\vecf{b} - \matr{A} \hat{\vecf{x}} = \paren{-\tfrac{1}{6}, \tfrac{1}{3}, -\tfrac{1}{6}}$
are orthogonal to both columns of $\matr{A}$:
$-\tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{1}{6} = 0$
and $-\tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{1}{2} = 0$.

:::
